families.s: HSE catering COSHH and cooking-fume control guidance
families.t: cooking fumes, oil mist, smoke, carbon monoxide, cleaning chemicals, substitution, ventilation, extractor hoods, PPE and hand care
f: Catering work can expose people to cooking fumes, oil mists, smoke and combustion products.
Gas-fired equipment can generate carbon monoxide if combustion or ventilation is inadequate.
Foods and cleaning-product ingredients can cause dermatitis, allergy or asthma.
Work techniques should minimise leaks, spills and direct contact with hazardous substances.
Cleaning products should be stored safely and used according to the assessed task.
Kitchen ventilation should remove fumes and vapours and discharge them safely outside.
Extractor hoods or canopies are normally required over cooking appliances.
PPE and hand care should supplement rather than replace effective process and ventilation controls.
families.g: Catering COSHH risk depends on fuel and appliance, food and chemical products, heat and cooking rate, ventilation and discharge, exposure route and duration, cleaning, PPE and maintenance.

families.s: HSE gas safety in catering and hospitality
families.t: gas-fired appliances, installation, maintenance, ventilation, flame failure, flues, isolation, competence and emergency action
f: HSE provides specific guidance on the safe use and maintenance of gas-fired catering equipment.
Kitchen ventilation is required to create a safe working environment and remove combustion products.
Adequate make-up air is particularly important for gas-fired appliances.
Incorrect flueing or insufficient air can cause incomplete combustion and carbon-monoxide accumulation.
Gas appliances and associated safety devices require planned maintenance.
Installation and servicing should be carried out by people competent for commercial catering gas work.
Emergency arrangements should include action for suspected gas leaks or unsafe combustion.
Caterers, building managers, designers and installers have connected duties when equipment or ventilation is changed.
families.g: Catering gas risk depends on appliance and fuel, combustion and flame safeguards, ventilation and make-up air, flues and discharge, installation, maintenance, isolation and competence.

families.t: heat, fumes, vapours, mechanical extraction, canopy design, make-up air, safe discharge, gas combustion, cleaning and maintenance
f: Commercial cooking can produce significant quantities of fumes, vapours and heat.
Kitchen ventilation should remove contaminants and provide a safe and comfortable environment.
Mechanical extraction is commonly provided through a canopy over cooking appliances.
The ventilation system should also provide general ventilation through the kitchen.
Replacement or make-up air should support effective extraction and safe combustion.
Extracted air should discharge to a safe external location.
Ventilation design should reflect the appliances, fuel and cooking process.
Canopies, filters, ducts and fans require cleaning, inspection and maintenance to remain effective.
families.g: Kitchen-ventilation risk control depends on appliance and cooking load, canopy capture, airflow and make-up air, discharge location, duct condition, cleaning frequency, noise, maintenance and competence.

families.s: HSE carbon-monoxide prevention for solid-fuel commercial kitchens
families.t: tandoori ovens, charcoal grills, wood-fired ovens, carbon monoxide, extraction, ventilation, public exposure, operation, maintenance and alarms
f: Solid-fuel appliances such as tandoori ovens, charcoal grills and wood-fired pizza ovens can create carbon-monoxide risk.
The risk applies to workers and members of the public in or near the premises.
Solid-fuel appliances produce carbon monoxide during normal operation.
An appropriate extraction system is needed to remove toxic combustion products.
Inadequate air supply or extraction can allow carbon monoxide to accumulate.
The employer should assess appliance use, ventilation and occupancy together.
Appliances, flues and extraction systems require planned inspection and maintenance.
Training and emergency arrangements should cover symptoms, alarms, unsafe combustion and evacuation.
families.g: Solid-fuel CO risk depends on appliance and fuel, combustion rate, ventilation and flue performance, room and public occupancy, maintenance, alarms, operator practices and emergency response.

families.s: HSE safe emptying and cleaning of commercial fryers
families.t: hot oil, cooling, automated and manual filtering, draining, containers, cleaning chemicals, slips, equipment and training
f: HSE provides specific guidance on safe emptying and cleaning of catering fryers.
The system should define when oil is cool enough for draining or cleaning.
Automated or semi-automated filtering can reduce manual handling of hot oil.
Manual oil filtering requires controlled draining, suitable equipment and safe containers.
Workers should be protected from burns, splashes and uncontrolled oil release.
Cleaning chemicals and water should be used without creating violent contact with hot oil.
Spill and slip risks should be controlled during draining and cleaning.
Workers need task-specific information, training and supervision.
families.g: Fryer-cleaning risk depends on oil temperature and volume, fryer and filter design, drain and container, water and chemicals, work area and flooring, PPE, maintenance and competence.
